Data pilot, 20 November 2026. Positions come from Otis's report of 1899 (the telegrams and their clock times), the January 1899 roster of the Eighth Army Corps, and the Signal Corps map of February 1899 with its index of final positions. Nothing here has been checked by a historian.

The Filipino side is thin: the sources read are American, and Taylor's notes on the Filipino commands around Manila date from August-September 1898. Every Filipino position is inferred, and the commanders named are those of 1898.
Many clock times are ranges: the reports give "early in the morning" or "during the afternoon". Telegram times (11:20, 12:30, about 16:30, 16:45) are exact to the minute.
The 1899 map is a blue-line photocopy drawn with north to the left, shown turned to north-up and fitted to today's ground to within about 170 m (at worst 270 m).
Symbols are blue for the Americans and red for the Filipino army; the colours are a drawing convention.

Ships are drawn where the reports read have them firing in support of the troops, landing men or carrying them. Their places on the water are estimates (the reports say "off" a town and no more), and this is the Army's account: no naval report was read.

Data pilot, 21 November 2026. One symbol is a column or a headquarters, placed at the town a report names on the date it gives. Positions are good to a kilometre or two at best. Nothing here has been checked by a historian.

American positions come from General Otis's two reports and their telegrams, Major Batson's report, and the dates printed on General Young's map. Where a date is a range ("during August", a blurred telegram date), the row says so and says which day the symbol is shown from.
The Filipino side is thin and comes from American reports: where the Republic's government and its main army were said to be. Strengths are American estimates. Much of it is inferred and marked so.

Aguinaldo's movements after 19 November, and the fight at Tirad Pass, are taken from Young's and March's reports as printed in a 1901 anti-imperialist pamphlet (the Philippine Information Society); the reports themselves were not found in the volumes read.
Operations south and east of Manila in 1899 (Paranaque and Zapote in June, Cavite in October) are not shown. The playback ends on 15 December; Lawton was killed at San Mateo on the 19th.

The three period maps are the Army's and the War Department's own. They were compiled from reconnaissance and older Spanish maps, not surveyed, so towns on them can be one to five kilometres from where they are; units are drawn at the true places.
Symbols are blue for the Americans and red for the Philippine Republic; the colours are a drawing convention.
